question: Where should an object be placed in front of a convex lens to get a real and enlarged image of the object ?
opt_c: Between the principal focus and twice the focal length
source_explanation_raw: Correct: C, Between the principal focus and twice the focal length. A convex lens produces an image that is both real and enlarged from only one object position, and the standard table of image formation shows which. Bring the object inside 2F but keep it outside F, and the image forms beyond 2F on the other side: real, inverted and larger than the object. Beyond 2F the image is real but diminished; at 2F it is the same size; at F no image forms, because the rays leave the lens parallel; inside F the image becomes virtual and erect. By the lens formula, the magnification of a real image is v/u in magnitude, so the image is larger than the object only when the image distance exceeds the object distance: precisely the band between F and 2F . A slide projector uses this setting, with the slide a little outside the focus and a big real picture on the distant screen.

question: The magnetic field lines inside a current carrying long solenoid are in the form of
source_explanation_raw: Correct: D, parallel straight lines. A solenoid is a long coil of insulated wire wound closely in the shape of a cylinder. Each turn contributes a circular field of its own, and along the axis of the coil those contributions add while the sideways parts of neighbouring turns cancel. What survives in the interior is a field of one strength pointing one way, so the field lines drawn there come out evenly spaced and parallel to the axis. NCERT states it in as many words: the field lines inside the solenoid are in the form of parallel straight lines, which indicates that the magnetic field is the same at all points inside the solenoid, that is, the field is uniform inside the solenoid. Outside, the picture is different: the lines crowd out of one end, loop round and re-enter the other, exactly as they do for a bar magnet, which is why one end of a current-carrying solenoid behaves as a north pole and the other as a south pole. Slide a soft-iron core inside and the same arrangement becomes an electromagnet.

question: A ray of light travelling from a rarer medium to a denser medium
opt_a: slows down and bends away from the normal.
opt_b: slows down and bends towards the normal.
opt_c: speeds up and bends away from the normal.
opt_d: speeds up and bends towards the normal.
source_explanation_raw: Correct: B, slows down and bends towards the normal. Denser and rarer here are optical descriptions, not statements about mass per unit volume: of two media, the one with the larger refractive index is the optically denser , and light travels more slowly in it. So a ray crossing from a rarer medium into a denser one loses speed at the boundary and bends towards the normal . The leading edge of the wavefront enters the new medium first and is slowed first, so the wavefront pivots, and that pivot is what an observer sees as a kink in the ray. Snell's law puts numbers on it: n1 sin i = n2 sin r, so with n2 greater than n1 the angle of refraction must be smaller than the angle of incidence. Going the other way, from denser to rarer, light speeds up and bends away from the normal.

question: An electric circuit is consisting of a cell, an ammeter and a nichrome wire of length l. If the length of the wire is reduced to half (l/2), then the ammeter reading
source_explanation_raw: Correct: B, gets doubled. For a uniform wire, resistance is proportional to length and inversely proportional to area of cross-section, so halving the length of the same nichrome wire halves its resistance . The cell holds the potential difference across the wire essentially fixed, and Ohm's law gives current as V divided by R: halve R and the current doubles . The ammeter is in series and reads that current, so its reading doubles. NCERT's Activity 11.3 sets up exactly this circuit (a cell, an ammeter, a nichrome wire of length l and a plug key) and records the mirror-image observation: the ammeter reading decreases to one-half when the length of the wire is doubled. The resistivity of nichrome is unaffected by cutting the wire; only the length has changed.

question: What is the effect of pressure of a human body on sand ?
opt_a: Larger while standing than while lying
opt_b: Smaller while standing than while lying
opt_d: Larger while standing during the daytime and smaller during the night time while lying
source_explanation_raw: Correct: A, Larger while standing than while lying. Pressure is thrust divided by the area over which the thrust acts, and thrust is the force acting perpendicular to the surface. In both postures the force pressing on the sand is the same: the person's weight . What changes is the contact area . Standing puts the whole weight on the soles of two feet, a few hundred square centimetres; lying down spreads it across the back or side, something like a square metre. The same weight over a much smaller area gives a much larger pressure, which is why feet sink into loose sand and a body lying on it does not. NCERT builds its section on pressure around exactly this comparison, noting that in both cases the force on the sand is the weight of the body.

question: An athlete completes one round of a circular track of diameter 100 m in 20 s. What will be the displacements after 1 minute and 10 s, respectively ?
source_explanation_raw: Correct: D, 0 m, 100 m. Displacement is the shortest distance from the starting position to the finishing position, so only where the athlete ends up matters, not how far they ran to get there. One lap takes 20 s. In 1 minute (60 s) the athlete completes exactly three laps and is back at the start, so the displacement is zero, even though 300 m of track has been covered. In 10 s the athlete runs half a lap and stands at the point diametrically opposite the start. The straight-line distance between those two points is the diameter of the circle, 100 m. The half-lap path length, half the circumference or about 157 m, is not among the options and is not what was asked.

question: Which of the following statements about universal indicator is/are true ? 1. It is a mixture of several indicators. 2. It shows different colours at different concentrations of hydrogen ions in solution. 3. It helps to determine the strength of given acid and base in titration. Select the correct answer using the code given below :
source_explanation_raw: Correct: D, 1, 2 and 3. Statements 1 and 2 are the textbook definition almost word for word: a universal indicator is a mixture of several indicators , and it shows different colours at different concentrations of hydrogen ions in a solution. Combining several dyes with different transition ranges is what lets a single strip run through a continuous sequence of colours instead of acting as one on-off switch, and matching that colour against a printed chart gives the pH. Statement 3 follows from what pH is for. Because the colour tracks hydrogen-ion concentration across the whole 0-to-14 range, a universal indicator lets you judge how strong a given acid or base is, not merely tell acid from base. Dilute hydrochloric acid and dilute ethanoic acid of the same concentration show different colours, because the first ionises far more completely.

question: Which of the following carbon allotropes is/are good conductor(s) of electricity? 1. Diamond 2. Graphite 3. Fullerene Select the correct answer using the code given below:
source_explanation_raw: Correct: C, 2 only. Graphite is the one allotrope on the list that conducts electricity well. Each carbon atom is bonded to only three neighbours in the same plane, forming hexagonal sheets stacked one above another, and that leaves one electron per atom free to move across the whole sheet. These delocalised electrons are what conduction requires, and the textbook states the point explicitly: graphite is a very good conductor of electricity, unlike other non-metals. Diamond bonds each carbon to four others in a rigid three-dimensional network, locking every valence electron into a bond, so it is an electrical insulator even though it is the best known conductor of heat. Fullerene C-60 is a closed cage of sixty carbon atoms shaped like a football. Its electrons are confined to individual molecules, and solid C-60 behaves as a semiconductor with a substantial band gap, not as a good conductor.

question: What is the approximate percentage of carbon in the Earth's crust?
source_explanation_raw: Correct: B, 0.025%. Carbon is everywhere in living matter and almost nowhere in the rocks. The standard textbook line is that the earth's crust has only 0.02% carbon , in minerals such as carbonates, hydrogen-carbonates, coal and petroleum, while the atmosphere holds about 0.03% carbon dioxide. Geochemical surveys of crustal abundance put the figure in the same narrow band, a couple of hundred parts per million, which is a few hundredths of one per cent. Of the four options, only 0.025% falls in that band. The contrast is worth more than the decimal: oxygen accounts for roughly 46% of the crust by mass and silicon for about 27%, so carbon, the element every living structure is built on, is only a trace constituent of rock.

question: When copper reacts with moist carbon dioxide (CO₂) in air, it forms a green coating of which one of the following compounds?
source_explanation_raw: Correct: A, Cupric carbonate. Copper left in damp air slowly loses its shiny brown surface and takes on a green coat. The textbook names the reaction directly: copper reacts with moist carbon dioxide in the air, and the green substance formed is basic copper carbonate . Of the four options, only cupric carbonate, copper in its plus-two state paired with the carbonate ion, belongs to that family, which is why the key takes it. The other three do not fit the stem: two are oxides of the wrong colour, and the third needs a sulphur source that moist carbon dioxide cannot supply.

question: What is the name of the process that converts sulphide ores into oxides by heating strongly in the presence of excess air?
source_explanation_raw: Correct: B, Roasting. The stem is the textbook definition word for word: sulphide ores are converted into oxides by heating strongly in the presence of excess air, and that process is called roasting . Zinc blende is the standard illustration: zinc sulphide heated in a current of air gives zinc oxide and sulphur dioxide. The step exists because a metal is far easier to recover from its oxide than from its sulphide or carbonate. So ores of the moderately reactive metals in the middle of the activity series, such as iron, zinc, lead and copper, are turned into oxides first and then reduced with carbon. Two words in the stem separate roasting from its twin: 'sulphide' and 'excess air'. A carbonate ore heated strongly in limited air is calcination .

question: What are the constituents of alloy solder?
source_explanation_raw: Correct: B, Pb and Sn. Solder is an alloy of lead and tin with a low melting point, used for joining electrical wires together, as the school text puts it in one sentence. That low melting point is its whole use. A tin-lead mixture near the eutectic composition, about sixty per cent tin to forty per cent lead, melts around 183 °C, well below either pure metal and far below the copper it joins, so the joint is made without damaging the wires or components. Lead brings a low melting point and good wetting; tin does the actual bonding to the copper surface. Restrictions on hazardous substances have pushed modern electronics largely towards lead-free solders of tin with silver and copper, but the tin-lead alloy is still what the syllabus means by solder.

question: Which of the following limits the number of trophic levels in a food chain?
opt_c: Decrease in the available energy at higher trophic levels
source_explanation_raw: Correct: C, Decrease in the available energy at higher trophic levels. Energy enters a food chain when green plants capture roughly one per cent of the sunlight falling on their leaves, and only about ten per cent of what is present at any step is passed on to the next. The rest is spent on the organism's own life processes or lost as heat. Because that loss happens again at every transfer, the energy left shrinks by a factor of about ten with each level, and after three or four steps too little remains to support another population. That is why food chains generally consist of only three or four steps . Energy also moves one way through the chain and never returns to a previous level, so what is lost cannot be recovered.

question: In pea, a pure tall plant (TT) is crossed with a short plant (tt). What will be the ratio of pure tall plants to short plants in the F₂ generation?
source_explanation_raw: Correct: A, 1 : 1. Cross a pure tall pea plant, genotype TT, with a short one, tt, and every plant of the first generation is Tt: tall, because a single copy of T is enough to make the plant tall, but carrying a hidden t. Self-pollinate that generation and each parent contributes T or t with equal probability, so the second generation comes out 1 TT : 2 Tt : 1 tt . The stem does not ask for tall against short, the familiar 3 : 1 of appearance; it asks for pure tall against short. Pure tall means TT alone, since Tt plants are tall but not pure-breeding, and short means tt. One quarter of the offspring are TT and one quarter are tt, so the ratio is 1 : 1. The safest habit is to write out the four boxes of the cross before reading the options.

question: Which one of the following statements about variations is not true?
opt_a: Variation is minimum in asexual reproduction.
opt_b: All variations in a species have equal chances of survival.
opt_c: Changes in genetic constitution result in variation.
opt_d: Variants can be selected by environmental factors.
source_explanation_raw: Correct: B, All variations in a species have equal chances of survival. The textbook asks this very question and answers it in the next sentence: do all the variations in a species have equal chances of surviving in the environment in which they find themselves? Obviously not. Depending on the nature of the variation, different individuals gain different advantages; the example given is bacteria able to withstand heat, which survive a heat wave better than their neighbours. Unequal survival is the whole point: if every variant did equally well, there would be nothing for the environment to select and evolution would have no engine. The other three statements are true as printed.

question: While studying vegetation of an area, terms like 'population' and 'community' are often used. Which one of the following statements best describes a population?
opt_a: A group of organisms of one species, living in the same area at the same time.
opt_b: A group of organisms of one species living in different areas during different seasons.
opt_c: A unit consisting of biotic and abiotic components.
opt_d: A group of organisms of more than one species, living in the same area at the same time.
source_explanation_raw: Correct: A, A group of organisms of one species, living in the same area at the same time. The standard textbook definition of a population is a group of individuals of a given species sharing or competing for similar resources in a defined geographical area, and every element of it appears in option (a). One species is the crucial restriction: the moment more than one species is involved, the correct word is community. A shared area matters, since individuals of one species on different continents do not compete for the same resources. The same time matters too: teak trees standing in a forest tract today and teak trees that stood there two centuries ago are not one population. Each textbook example, such as all the cormorants in a wetland, is one species, one place, one time.

question: In the human body, blood flows through a process of double circulation. Which one of the following statements is true in this regard?
opt_a: Oxygenated blood reaches the left side of the heart from the lungs.
opt_b: Blood in the left side of the heart is poor in oxygen and is brought to the right side of the heart.
opt_c: Deoxygenated blood from the left side of the heart is brought to the lungs for oxygenation.
opt_d: Oxygenated blood from the right side of the heart is sent around the body.
source_explanation_raw: Correct: A, Oxygenated blood reaches the left side of the heart from the lungs. Oxygen-rich blood coming back from the lungs enters the thin-walled left atrium , which relaxes to collect it and then contracts to pass it to the left ventricle. The muscular left ventricle pumps that blood out to the whole body. Blood returning from the body, now de-oxygenated, arrives in the right atrium, passes to the right ventricle and is sent from there to the lungs to be oxygenated. The blood thus passes through the heart twice in one complete circuit, which is what double circulation names. Keeping the two sides separate prevents mixing and allows a highly efficient supply of oxygen, which birds and mammals need because they spend energy constantly to keep their body temperature steady.

question: In which of the following groups of organisms, is food material broken down outside the body and absorbed?
source_explanation_raw: Correct: A, Yeast, mushroom, bread mould. Breaking food down outside the body and then absorbing the products is saprophytic nutrition , and it is what fungi do. A bread mould growing on a slice of bread secretes digestive enzymes onto it, the enzymes dissolve the starch and protein where they lie, and the fungus takes up the soluble products through its hyphae ; yeast and mushrooms feed the same way. The textbook sentence behind this item names exactly that trio: some organisms break down the food material outside the body and then absorb it, examples being fungi like bread moulds, yeast and mushrooms. The wrong options are built from the other feeding strategies in the same passage: parasites that feed on a living host, single-celled feeders that digest food internally, and green plants that make their own food.

question: A sound wave has a frequency of 4 kHz and wavelength 30 cm. How long will it take to travel 2·4 km?
source_explanation_raw: Correct: A, 2·0 s. Work out the speed first and the time falls out. The speed of a wave is its wavelength multiplied by its frequency : with a frequency of 4 kHz (4000 hertz) and a wavelength of 30 cm (0·30 m), the speed is 4000 × 0·30 = 1200 metres per second. The journey is 2·4 km, which is 2400 m, and time is distance divided by speed: 2400 ÷ 1200 = 2 s. Two habits keep this safe. Convert everything into metres and seconds before multiplying, since a stray centimetre or kilometre is the usual source of a factor of a hundred or a thousand. And check that 1200 m/s is plausible: faster than sound in air at about 343 m/s, but slower than in steel at nearly 6000 m/s.

question: An electric bulb is connected to a 110 V generator. The current is 0·2 A. What is the power of the bulb?
source_explanation_raw: Correct: C, 22 W. Electric power is the rate at which electrical energy is consumed, and for a device carrying a steady current it is the potential difference across it multiplied by the current through it: P equals V times I . Substituting the stem's numbers, 110 volts multiplied by 0·2 ampere gives 22 watts. The watt is defined so that this multiplication works directly: one watt is the power consumed by a device carrying one ampere at a potential difference of one volt. The only place to slip is the decimal in the current . Two cross-checks help. The implied resistance, V divided by I, is 550 ohms, a sensible figure for a small lamp. And the options are all the same digits with the decimal moved, so make sure to multiply by 0·2, not by 2 or 0·02.

question: Refraction of light, as it enters from one transparent medium to another, is due to
opt_a: change in temperature of the media.
opt_b: change in the amplitude of light.
source_explanation_raw: Correct: C, change in speed of light. Refraction happens because light does not travel at the same speed in every transparent medium, and the textbook says so in one line: refraction is due to change in the speed of light as it enters from one transparent medium to another. Picture the wavefront rather than the ray. When a broad wavefront meets the boundary at an angle, one edge crosses into the new medium first and immediately travels at the new speed, so the wavefront pivots and the direction of travel swings: towards the normal where the second medium is slower, away from it where it is faster. This is also why refractive index is defined as a ratio of speeds , and why a ray entering along the normal changes speed without changing direction: a wavefront meeting the boundary square-on has no edge that arrives first.

question: A bus starting from a bus-stand and moving with uniform acceleration attains a speed of 20 km/h in 10 minutes. What is its acceleration?
source_explanation_raw: Correct: B, 120 km/h². Acceleration is the change in velocity divided by the time taken . The bus starts from rest, so the initial speed is zero and the change in speed is the full 20 km/h. The awkward part is the time, which is given in minutes while the options are in kilometres per hour squared, so the units have to agree before dividing. Ten minutes is one-sixth of an hour , and dividing 20 km/h by one-sixth of an hour is the same as multiplying by six, which gives 120 km/h². The number reads oddly, but it says something ordinary: if this rate were kept up for a whole hour, the bus would gain 120 km/h of speed. In SI units, 20 km/h is about 5·56 m/s and 10 minutes is 600 s, giving roughly 0·0093 m/s², which converts straight back to 120 km/h².

question: Which one of the following is the correct reactivity order of metals reacting with dilute HCl?
source_explanation_raw: Correct: A, Mg > Al > Zn > Fe. The four metals are being ranked by how readily they react with dilute hydrochloric acid, and the answer is read straight off the activity series, which lists metals in order of decreasing reactivity: potassium, sodium, calcium, magnesium, aluminium, zinc, iron, lead, then hydrogen, then copper, mercury, silver and gold. Every metal above hydrogen in that list can push hydrogen out of a dilute acid, and the higher it stands the more vigorously it does so. Take the four in the question in the order the series prints them and magnesium comes first, then aluminium, then zinc, then iron, which is option (a) exactly. The laboratory picture matches: magnesium ribbon fizzes hard in dilute hydrochloric acid and the tube warms noticeably, zinc gives a steady stream of bubbles, iron reacts slowly, and aluminium behaves erratically at first because a tough oxide film has to be broken through before the metal underneath is reached. Copper, sitting below hydrogen, gives no hydrogen with dilute hydrochloric acid at all.

question: Which one of the following acids is secreted by leaves of Nettle that causes painful stings?
source_explanation_raw: Correct: A, Methanoic acid. The stinging hairs of the nettle leaf inject methanoic acid , and that is what produces the burning pain. Methanoic acid is the systematic name of what is more often called formic acid ; the older name comes from formica, Latin for ant, since an ant's bite delivers the same compound. Each hair works like a tiny hypodermic needle: brush against the leaf and the brittle silica tip snaps off, leaving a sharp open tube that pierces the skin and releases the irritant fluid beneath. Because the injected substance is an acid, the traditional remedies are all mild bases: rubbing the spot with the leaf of the dock plant, which often grows beside the nettle, or dabbing on baking soda. The same neutralising chemistry is used against a bee sting, which is also acidic.

question: Which of the following statements is/are correct? 1. All the bases are alkali. 2. All alkalis dissolve in water. 3. Alkalis are soapy to touch, bitter in taste and corrosive in nature. Select the correct answer using the code given below:
source_explanation_raw: Correct: C, 2 and 3 only. Statement 1 reverses the relationship between the two words. Bases generate hydroxide ions in water, and the textbook is explicit that all bases do not dissolve in water: an alkali is a base that dissolves in water. So every alkali is a base, but not every base is an alkali; copper hydroxide and iron hydroxide are bases that stay insoluble. Statement 2 is true by that same definition, since dissolving in water is what earns a base the name alkali . Statement 3 lists the three properties the textbook gives alkalis in one sentence (soapy to touch, bitter and corrosive), together with the warning never to taste or touch them, because they can cause harm. Drawn as sets, alkalis form a smaller circle inside the larger circle of bases.

question: Which one of the following materials is present in a guard tube (drying tube) that is used for preparation of HCl gas?
source_explanation_raw: Correct: A, Calcium chloride. The guard tube in this arrangement has one job, to keep the hydrogen chloride gas dry, and the material packed into it is calcium chloride . The laboratory note for the preparation says that if the climate is very humid, the gas produced has to be passed through a guard tube, also called a drying tube, containing calcium chloride to dry it. Anhydrous calcium chloride is chosen because it is a powerful drying agent , taking up water vapour readily and holding it, and because it does not react with hydrogen chloride, which rules out most of the alternatives a chemist might reach for. Drying matters because the experiment shows that dry hydrogen chloride gas has no acidic character (it leaves dry litmus paper unchanged). Acidity appears only when water is present, because the hydrogen ion cannot separate from the hydrogen chloride molecule without it.

question: Fertilizers are used to obtain higher yields of crops. However, all nutrients are usually not available in fertilizers. Which one of the following nutrients is usually not available in fertilizers?
source_explanation_raw: Correct: A, Iron. Fertilizers are commercially produced plant nutrients, and what they supply is nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium : the three that plants need in the largest quantities and that soils run short of first. Three of the four options are on that list; iron is not. Iron is certainly essential to plants, taking part in chlorophyll synthesis and in the electron carriers of photosynthesis, but it is a micronutrient , required only in small quantities. Ordinary bagged fertilizer targets the macronutrients, which is why its shorthand is N-P-K. Micronutrient shortages, when they occur, are usually corrected by manure, by a dedicated micronutrient mixture or by a foliar spray, not by the general-purpose fertilizer the stem has in mind.

question: Rupa and Sachin observed an animal in their school garden. Rupa called it an insect while Sachin identified it as an earthworm. Which one of the following characteristics confirms that it is an insect ?
opt_b: Body of the animal had very little segmentation.
opt_c: Body of the animal was cylindrical.
opt_d: Body of the animal was bilaterally symmetrical.
source_explanation_raw: Correct: A, The animal had jointed legs. Jointed legs are the defining feature of the arthropods , the group insects belong to; the word arthropod is built from the Greek for jointed foot. The standard description says these animals are bilaterally symmetrical and segmented, and that they have jointed legs. An earthworm is an annelid and has no legs at all , jointed or otherwise, so the moment jointed legs are observed the identification is settled in Rupa's favour. The other three characteristics are why the disagreement was possible, because insects and earthworms share every one of them. Both are bilaterally symmetrical, both have a cylindrical body plan, and both are segmented: the earthworm's segments are lined up one behind another from head to tail, while an insect is divided into head, thorax and abdomen.

question: Animals which are marine, bilaterally symmetrical, have a coelom and a notochord, but never form a vertebral column are placed under which one of the following groups ?
source_explanation_raw: Correct: B, Protochordata. The stem is a checklist of the standard description, item by item. Protochordates are bilaterally symmetrical, triploblastic and have a coelom; they show a new feature of body design, a notochord , at least at some stages during their lives; and they are marine animals. The last clause of the stem is what excludes the more inclusive answers: these animals never form a vertebral column , which is precisely the line between the protochordates and the vertebrates. Vertebrates are defined by a true vertebral column and an internal skeleton, so an animal that never develops one cannot be placed there.

question: What is the location of intercalary meristem in plants ?
opt_a: Base of the leaves or internodes
source_explanation_raw: Correct: A, Base of the leaves or internodes. Meristematic tissue is the dividing tissue of a plant, and it is classified by position. Apical meristem is at the growing tips of stems and roots and lengthens them; lateral meristem, the cambium, sits along the sides and thickens the stem or root. Intercalary meristem is the third kind, so called because it is intercalated (inserted) between mature tissues rather than sitting at a tip, and its position is near the node , at the base of the leaves or at the base of the internodes. Grasses are where it matters most. A grass or a cereal grows from these basal zones rather than from the tip, which is why a lawn keeps growing after mowing and why grazing does not kill pasture: the growing region lies below where the blade is cut or bitten off. Bamboo, one of the fastest-growing plants, extends by division at exactly these zones above each node.

question: The federation of which one of the following States has been described as “an indestructible union of indestructible states” ?
source_explanation_raw: Correct: B, U.S.A. The phrase is a quotation from Chief Justice Salmon P. Chase's opinion for the United States Supreme Court in Texas v. White (1869) , decided while the country was working out what the Civil War had settled: “The Constitution, in all its provisions, looks to an indestructible Union, composed of indestructible States.” Texas had purported to secede in 1861 and then sued to recover United States bonds sold by its Confederate government. The Court held that the ordinance of secession was legally void, that Texas had never ceased to be a State, and that the Union could not be broken by any State acting alone. The two halves do different work. The Union is indestructible because no State may leave it unilaterally; the States are indestructible because the federal government cannot abolish or reshape them at will . India is built the other way round on the second half, which is exactly why this item is set.

question: Who among the following is the author of the famous essay, ‘The End of History and the Last Man’ ?
source_explanation_raw: Correct: A, Francis Fukuyama. Fukuyama first made the argument in an essay called ‘The End of History?’ in the summer 1989 issue of The National Interest, months before the Berlin Wall came down, and expanded it into the 1992 book The End of History and the Last Man. His claim was never that events would stop happening. It was that the long argument about which principles should organise a modern state had run out of serious contenders: with the collapse of communism, Western liberal democracy stood as “the end point of mankind's ideological evolution and the universalization of Western liberal democracy as the final form of human government”. The second half of the title comes from the other side of his own case: the ‘last man’ is Nietzsche's figure, borrowed to ask whether people whose recognition and material wants are satisfied will still find life worth striving in. Fukuyama built the framework on Hegel as read through Alexandre Kojève, which is why the thesis is about the direction of history rather than about any particular election.

question: Which one of the following statements is not correct ?
opt_a: Allahabad High Court has a Bench at Lucknow.
opt_b: Madhya Pradesh High Court has a Bench at Gwalior.
opt_c: Rajasthan High Court is located at Jodhpur.
opt_d: Guwahati High Court has no Bench.
source_explanation_raw: Correct: D, Guwahati High Court has no Bench. The court, whose principal seat is at Guwahati, has three permanent Benches : Kohima for Nagaland, set up on 1 December 1972; Aizawl for Mizoram, from 5 July 1990; and Itanagar for Arunachal Pradesh, from 12 August 2000. That is the point of the institution: it is one of the few High Courts with jurisdiction over several States , so it has to sit where the litigants are. The other three statements are sound, and since only one statement can be false, the Guwahati claim is the answer.

question: Which among the following is not a condition for the disqualification of a Member of Parliament ?
opt_a: Voluntary acquisition of citizenship of a foreign country
opt_b: Holding the office of the Chairperson of the National Commission for Women
opt_c: The Member abstains from voting in the House without prior permission
opt_d: The Member holds the office of the Chairman of the Board of Directors of the National Coal Development Corporation Ltd.
source_explanation_raw: Correct: B, Holding the office of the Chairperson of the National Commission for Women. Article 102(1)(a) disqualifies a Member for holding an office of profit under the Government of India or of a State, but it carries its own escape clause: “other than an office declared by Parliament by law not to disqualify its holder”. That law is the Parliament (Prevention of Disqualification) Act, 1959 , and its section 3 lists the protected offices. The Chairperson of the National Commission for Women, constituted under section 3 of the National Commission for Women Act, 1990, is on that list, alongside the chairpersons and members of the other national commissions. So this office attracts no disqualification, while each of the other three options names a ground that does.

question: Who among the following considered the Directive Principles of State Policy as aiming at 'furthering the goals of social exclusion'?
source_explanation_raw: Correct: B, Granville Austin. Austin is the American historian of the Indian Constitution whose The Indian Constitution: Cornerstone of a Nation (1966) supplied the vocabulary that Indian polity texts still use for Part IV. His reading is that the Constituent Assembly wrote two revolutions into the document (a political one, carried by the Fundamental Rights, and a social and economic one, carried by the Directive Principles) and that the two together form what he called the conscience of the Constitution. On that account the Directive Principles are not decorative; they are the instrument by which the State is meant to carry the social revolution forward, which is why Article 37 calls them fundamental in the governance of the country even while making them unenforceable in a court. None of the other three names is associated with that formulation.

question: D performs her train journey by the shortest route from Bengaluru to New Delhi. Which one of the following rivers will she not cross while performing the journey?
source_explanation_raw: Correct: B, Yamuna. Read the journey as a line drawn north from the Deccan and ask which rivers lie across it. Bengaluru sits on the Mysore plateau south of the Krishna, and every rail route north from there runs up the peninsula and across central India before turning for Delhi. The Krishna and the Godavari both rise in the Western Ghats and flow eastward to the Bay of Bengal, so they cut the route squarely; the Godavari crossing is one of the landmarks of the journey whichever of the two main alignments the train takes. Further north the Narmada runs the other way, west to the Arabian Sea through its rift valley, and the line crosses it near Itarsi. The Yamuna is different in kind. It comes down from Yamunotri, runs south past Delhi, Mathura and Agra, and the railway to the capital runs beside it rather than over it: the Agra–Mathura–Faridabad main line and New Delhi station all lie on the right, western bank. The traveller does cross the Chambal, a Yamuna tributary, before Agra, but reaches New Delhi without ever crossing the Yamuna itself.

question: Identify the State on the basis of the following characteristics: 1. Tropic of Cancer passes through the State. 2. The State has more north-south extension. 3. The State has international border with Bangladesh and Myanmar. Select the correct answer using the code given below:
source_explanation_raw: Correct: B, Mizoram. Take the three clues in turn and only one State survives all of them. The Tropic of Cancer crosses eight Indian States, including Tripura and Mizoram, which at once removes Nagaland and Manipur, both of which lie wholly north of it. The shape clue then favours Mizoram: its maximum north-south distance is about 285 km against a maximum east-west stretch of about 115 km, a long narrow State running down the hills, while Tripura is a compact block. The border clue is decisive on its own. Mizoram's 722 km of international boundary is shared with Bangladesh on the west and Myanmar on the east and south; Tripura touches Myanmar nowhere.

question: M wants to visit a place in a Union Territory, which is located at 34° N and 77° E. Which one of the following Union Territories must he have planned to visit?
source_explanation_raw: Correct: D, Ladakh. The coordinates do the whole job. Leh stands at about 34 degrees 09 minutes north and 77 degrees 35 minutes east, at roughly 3,500 metres, so a point given as 34 degrees north and 77 degrees east falls inside Ladakh. Nothing else on the list is even close. Ladakh is the only Union Territory of India that lies north of 30 degrees north; the other three are all tropical and lie far to the east or the west of 77 degrees. Ladakh became a Union Territory on 31 October 2019 under the Jammu and Kashmir Reorganisation Act, 2019, with Leh and Kargil as its two capitals, which is what makes the item answerable in the form it is asked, since before that date the same coordinates would have named a district of a State.

question: Consider the following statements with respect to the adolescent population (age group of 10 to 19 years) of India, according to the 2011 Census: 1. Adolescent population comprises half the population of the country. 2. The group is regarded as youthful population with high potential. 3. In this group there are greater number of females than males. Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
source_explanation_raw: Correct: B, 2 only. The question follows the school text almost word for word, and the text settles all three claims. Statement 1 is far out: adolescents aged 10 to 19 were about 20.9 per cent of India's population at the 2011 Census, roughly a fifth, not a half. Statement 3 fails on sex composition: male adolescents were 52.7 per cent and female adolescents 47.3 per cent, so there are more males, the same imbalance that shows up in India's child sex ratio. Statement 2 survives: the group is treated as a youthful population of high potential , while also being described as vulnerable if it is not guided properly.

question: In a discussion, M from Arunachal Pradesh, J from Assam, N from Meghalaya and S from Nagaland are claiming that as per Census 2011, their State has the maximum density of population. Identify the person making the correct claim.
source_explanation_raw: Correct: B, J. J is from Assam, and at the 2011 Census Assam's population density was 398 persons per square kilometre, not merely the highest of the four, but higher than the other three put together. Meghalaya stood at 132, Nagaland at 119 and Arunachal Pradesh at 17, the lowest figure for any State in India. The reason is physical. Assam holds the broad alluvial floodplains of the Brahmaputra and the Barak, land that can be cropped intensively and settled densely, while Meghalaya sits on a plateau and Nagaland and Arunachal Pradesh are steep, forested hill States where cultivable flat land is scarce. Assam is also much the most populous of the four, with over 31 million people in 2011 against about 3 million in Meghalaya, under 2 million in Nagaland and under 1.4 million in Arunachal Pradesh.

question: Who among the following ancient Indian kings was praised in glowing terms in the Prayaga Prashasti?
source_explanation_raw: Correct: C, Samudragupta. The Prayaga Prashasti, better known as the Allahabad Pillar Inscription, is a Sanskrit eulogy composed by Harishena, the court poet of Samudragupta, in about the fourth century CE. It is the single most important source for that reign: it lists the kings of Aryavarta whom he uprooted, the rulers of Dakshinapatha whom he defeated and then reinstated, the forest kingdoms he reduced to servitude, and the frontier states and foreign powers that offered submission, and it does all this in the high poetic register of prashasti literature, praising the king as one without an antagonist on earth. Because prashastis are compositions in praise rather than reports, historians read them for the shape of a reign while discounting the flattery, and this inscription is the standard classroom example of that method.

question: The Self-Respect Movement was initiated by
source_explanation_raw: Correct: C, E. V. Ramaswamy Naicker. The Self-Respect Movement began in Tamil country in 1925 and is inseparable from the man everyone calls Periyar. Its programme was rationalist and anti-caste at the same time: it attacked the ritual authority of the Brahmin priesthood, rejected the religious sanction claimed for caste hierarchy, and argued that a person who acquires self-respect stops being led by others. Its most concrete innovation was the self-respect marriage, conducted without a Brahmin priest and without Vedic rites: the first fully non-religious ceremony of the kind was performed on 8 December 1929 with Periyar presiding, and Tamil Nadu gave such marriages statutory recognition in 1967 by amending the Hindu Marriage Act for the State. Periyar had left the Congress in the mid-1920s over precisely these questions, and the movement he built became the seedbed of Dravidian politics.

question: The location of the ancient city of Taxila (Takshshila), mentioned in ancient Indian texts, was identified by
source_explanation_raw: Correct: A, Alexander Cunnigham. Taxila had been famous in Sanskrit, Pali and Greek sources for centuries: as Takshashila in Indian texts and Taxila in the accounts that came down from Alexander's campaign, but nobody knew where it had stood. Alexander Cunningham, the founder and first Director-General of the Archaeological Survey of India, matched the descriptions and distances given by the Chinese pilgrims against the ground north-west of Rawalpindi and identified the ruins there as Taxila in 1863 to 1864. That is the act the question is asking about: an identification made from texts and topography, not an excavation. Half a century later Sir John Marshall began digging the sites, working there over twenty years from 1913 and uncovering the successive cities of Bhir Mound, Sirkap and Sirsukh. Note that the booklet prints the surname as Cunnigham, a slip of a letter, and Takshshila for Takshashila.

question: Who among the following was not a Jain Acharya?
source_explanation_raw: Correct: B, Khema. Khema belongs to the other heterodox tradition altogether. She was a Buddhist bhikkhuni of the sixth century BCE, born at Sagala, daughter of the king of Madra and married to Bimbisara of Magadha; the Buddha named her foremost in wisdom among his female disciples, and she is counted with Uppalavanna as one of his two chief nuns, the counterpart of Sariputta on the men's side. Her verses survive in the Therigatha, the collection of poems by elder Buddhist nuns, and she is listed in the Anguttara Nikaya among the leading women followers. The other three are all Jain teachers of the first rank: Bhadrabahu, the last Shruta Kevalin; Haribhadra, the great Sanskrit and Prakrit author of the eighth century; and Siddhasena Divakara, the logician. Khema is the intruder.

question: In India, the first major public appearance of Mahatma Gandhi was in
source_explanation_raw: Correct: C, Inauguration of Banaras Hindu University (1916). Gandhi returned from South Africa in January 1915 and, on Gokhale's advice, spent his first year travelling the country rather than speaking in it. His first major public appearance came at the opening of the Banaras Hindu University in February 1916, an occasion attended by princes, philanthropists and Congress leaders including Annie Besant, where he was still relatively unknown and had been invited on the strength of his South African work. When his turn came he attacked the assembled elite for their indifference to the labouring poor, called the ceremony a most gorgeous show, contrasted the richly bedecked noblemen present with the millions of the poor who were absent, and told them there could be no self-government while the peasant's produce was taken from him. That speech, not any of the campaigns, is the moment the question is pointing at.

question: Consider the following statements about Patanjali's Mahabhashya: 1. It makes a mention of Kautilya. 2. It is a book on grammar and refers to historical personalities only incidentally. Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
source_explanation_raw: Correct: B, 2 only. Patanjali's Mahabhashya, composed in about the mid-second century BCE, is a commentary on selected rules of Panini's Ashtadhyayi together with Katyayana's varttikas on them. It is a work of vyakarana from beginning to end, and everything historical in it arrives sideways: as illustrative sentences chosen to demonstrate a form, a tense or a case. That is exactly what statement 2 claims, and it is the reason historians prize the text: an incidental remark about a recent Greek incursion is one of the fixed points used to date the work itself. Statement 1 is the one the key rejects. The Mahabhashya is not among the texts that carry the name Kautilya; that name reaches us from the Arthashastra itself and from later literature such as the Puranas and Vishakhadatta's play Mudrarakshasa. So the second statement stands alone.

question: Which one of the following may lead to movement along the demand curve of a commodity?
opt_b: Change in price of the other commodities
opt_c: Change in income of the consumer
opt_d: Change in tastes and preferences of consumers
source_explanation_raw: Correct: A, Change in its price. A demand curve is drawn with the commodity's own price on one axis and the quantity demanded on the other, and everything else (income, the prices of other goods, tastes, the number of buyers, expectations) is held fixed while it is drawn. So a change in the commodity's own price cannot move the curve; it can only move the buyer to a different point on the same curve. That is what movement along the demand curve means, and textbooks give the two directions their own names: a fall in price produces an extension of demand down the curve, a rise produces a contraction up it. Every other item on the list is one of the things held constant while the curve was drawn, so a change in any of them redraws the curve at a new position: a shift, not a movement.

question: Which one of the following is the opportunity cost of a chosen activity?
opt_b: Out of pocket cost plus cost incurred by the Government
opt_d: Value of next best alternative that is given up
source_explanation_raw: Correct: D, Value of next best alternative that is given up. Opportunity cost is what economics substitutes for the accountant's idea of cost. Because resources are scarce, choosing one use of them means abandoning every other use; the cost of the chosen activity is measured by the value of the best of those abandoned uses, and by that one alone. The word next is doing the work. If a person can spend an hour studying, working for two hundred rupees, or sleeping, and ranks the paid work second after studying, then the cost of studying is two hundred rupees, not the sleep as well, and not the sum of both. Measured this way, cost includes things no ledger records, which is why a self-employed shopkeeper's true cost includes the salary he could have earned elsewhere, and why a free public service still costs society something.

question: Which one of the following statements in the context of social sector spending in India during 2014–19 (both States and the Union Government together) is true?
opt_a: Expenditure on education was 5% of GDP.
opt_b: Expenditure on health was 4% of the social services expenditure.
opt_c: There was a stagnation in the spending on education as a percent of GDP.
opt_d: Health sector spending amounted to 10% of the total expenditure.
source_explanation_raw: Correct: C, There was a stagnation in the spending on education as a percent of GDP. Taking the Centre and the States together, general government spending on education stayed inside a narrow band of roughly 2.8 to 3.1 per cent of GDP across 2014-15 to 2019-20. It had been about 3.1 per cent in 2013-14, settled near 2.8 per cent through the middle of the period and edged back to about 2.9 per cent at the end. A share that moves by two or three tenths of a percentage point over six years while the economy grows is the textbook picture of stagnation . That is why the six per cent of GDP target first set in 1968 has stayed out of reach. The other three options are quantitative claims that the same series contradicts.

question: According to UNDP's Human Development Report – 2020, in which of the HDI components has India improved in recent years? 1. Life expectancy at birth 2. Expected years of schooling 3. GNI per capita 4. Mean years of schooling Select the correct answer using the code given below :
source_explanation_raw: Correct: C, 1 and 3 only. The Human Development Index has three dimensions and four indicators. The 2020 Report put India at a life expectancy at birth of 69.7 years, expected years of schooling of 12.2, mean years of schooling of 6.5 and GNI per capita of 6,681 international dollars at 2017 purchasing power parity. Of those four, the two still moving in the years immediately before the Report were life expectancy , which had continued its slow climb, and per-capita income , which had continued to rise on the Report's own recomputed series. The two schooling measures had gone flat, neither rising from edition to edition, which is why the key pairs statement 1 with statement 3.

question: Which one of the following is true of a pure voluntary exchange between two parties A and B?
opt_a: A can exploit B or vice versa
opt_b: Both gain; it is a win-win situation
opt_c: If A makes profit, it must be at the cost of B
source_explanation_raw: Correct: B, Both gain; it is a win-win situation. The word doing the work in the stem is voluntary. If neither party is forced and both are informed, each will agree only if what is received is worth more to that party than what is given up: otherwise the offer would simply be refused. So the very fact that an exchange takes place is evidence that both sides expect to be better off, and the difference between what each values in and out is the gain from trade. That is why economists reject the older mercantilist picture in which one side's profit must be the other's loss: exchange is not a transfer of a fixed stock of value but a rearrangement that raises the value of the same goods by moving them to whoever values them more. The theory says both gain; it does not say the gains are equal or fairly divided, and that is a separate question.

question: The provision, ‘the State shall take steps to separate the Judiciary from the Executive in the public services of the State’ is incorporated in which part of the Constitution of India?
source_explanation_raw: Correct: A, Part-IV. The words quoted are Article 50 of the Constitution, and Article 50 sits in Part IV, the Directive Principles of State Policy, which runs from Article 36 to Article 51. The placement carries a consequence. Under Article 37 the Directive Principles are not enforceable by any court, so no litigant could have sued a State into separating its magistracy from its district administration; the separation had to be carried out by legislation and administrative reorganisation instead, which is what happened when the Code of Criminal Procedure was recast in 1973, splitting the old office of magistrate into judicial magistrates under the High Court and executive magistrates under the State government. The Article is usually grouped with the liberal-intellectual Directive Principles rather than the socialist or Gandhian ones.

question: Which of the following statements are correct? 1. Speaker may permit any Member to address the House in his/her mother tongue, if he/she cannot adequately express in either Hindi or English. 2. Business of the Parliamentary Committees is transacted either in Hindi or in English. 3. The minutes of the Parliamentary Committees are prepared invariably in Hindi or English. Select the correct answer using the code given below :
source_explanation_raw: Correct: A, 1, 2 and 3. All three statements describe the settled language regime of Parliament and its committees. Statement 1 is the proviso to Article 120(1) : the Chairman of the Council of States or the Speaker of the House of the People “may permit any member who cannot adequately express himself in Hindi or in English to address the House in his mother-tongue”. The permission is discretionary. Statements 2 and 3 carry that regime into the committees. A parliamentary committee is a creature of the House and works under its Rules of Procedure, so its business is transacted in Hindi or in English, and its record is prepared invariably in one of those two languages , whatever language a member or witness spoke. The reason is practical: the minutes and report must be usable by the whole House, the Government and any court that later reads them.

question: Which one of the following is the correct meaning of the term ‘State’, as defined in Article 12 of the Constitution of India?
opt_a: It refers only to the Government of India.
opt_b: It refers only to the Government of India and the Parliament of India.
opt_c: It refers only to the Government of India, Parliament of India, and Governments and Legislatures of each State.
opt_d: It refers to the Government of India, Parliament of India, Governments and Legislatures of each State, and all local or other authorities within the territory of India.
source_explanation_raw: Correct: D, It refers to the Government of India, Parliament of India, Governments and Legislatures of each State, and all local or other authorities within the territory of India. Article 12 is a definition clause, and it is deliberately the widest of the four options. It says that in Part III, unless the context otherwise requires, the State includes the Government and Parliament of India, the Government and the Legislature of each of the States, and all local or other authorities within the territory of India or under the control of the Government of India. The breadth is the point: Fundamental Rights are guaranteed against the State, so if the definition were confined to the Union executive a citizen could not enforce Article 14 against a municipality, a State legislature or a statutory corporation. The last limb, all local or other authorities, is where the definition has grown most: the courts have read other authorities to cover statutory bodies and, through the instrumentality-or-agency test, government companies and societies that are financially, functionally and administratively dominated by the government.

question: Which one among the following is the largest State in terms of seats in the Rajya Sabha?
source_explanation_raw: Correct: B, Bihar. Rajya Sabha seats are allotted State by State in the Fourth Schedule, broadly according to population, and among the four names offered Bihar has the most with 16. Karnataka comes next with 12, Andhra Pradesh has 11 and Rajasthan 10. Two reorganisations lie behind those numbers and are worth carrying: Bihar had 22 seats until Jharkhand was carved out of it in 2000, and Andhra Pradesh had 18 until Telangana was separated in 2014, taking 7 of them. Note the limit of the claim: Bihar is the largest of these four, not of the country. Uttar Pradesh has 31, followed by Maharashtra with 19 and Tamil Nadu with 18, so Bihar is fourth nationally, level with West Bengal.

question: Under which Article of the Constitution of India has provision been made for reservation of seats for women in Panchayats?
source_explanation_raw: Correct: C, Article 243 D. Part IX of the Constitution, inserted by the Seventy-third Amendment in 1992, runs from Article 243 to Article 243-O, and each Article in the opening run has one job. Article 243D is the reservation Article. Clause (1) reserves seats for the Scheduled Castes and the Scheduled Tribes in every panchayat in proportion to their share of the population, and clause (2) gives not less than one-third of those reserved seats to SC and ST women. Clause (3) is the general women's quota: not less than one-third of the seats filled by direct election in every panchayat, inclusive of the clause (2) seats. Clause (4) carries the same reservations into the offices of chairperson.

question: The painted illustration of the moving of the Ashoka Pillar at Topra is found in
source_explanation_raw: Correct: C, Sirat-i-Firuz Shahi. Firuz Shah Tughlaq, who ruled from Delhi between 1351 and 1388, had two Ashokan pillars brought to his capital: one from Topra in present-day Haryana and one from Meerut. The Topra shaft was moved in the 1350s and re-erected beside the Friday mosque of his new city of Firuzabad. The operation was a feat of medieval engineering: the pillar was wrapped in silk cotton and then in reeds and raw hide, lowered onto a cart of forty-two wheels with two hundred men to a wheel, and floated down the Yamuna on boats. The Sirat-i-Firuz Shahi, an anonymous contemporary chronicle of the Sultan's reign written in the fourteenth century, records the move and carries the painted illustration of it that the question is asking about: one of the earliest depictions of an engineering operation in Indian manuscript painting.

question: Which one among the following is a temple of the Vaishnavite tradition?
source_explanation_raw: Correct: A, Srirangam. The Ranganathaswamy temple at Srirangam is dedicated to Ranganatha , the reclining form of Vishnu, with his consort Ranganayaki, and it is the foremost of the hundred and eight Divya Desams , the shrines sung by the Alvar poet-saints. It stands on the island between the Kaveri and its distributary the Kollidam, and it was the institutional centre of Ramanuja's Sri Vaishnavism: he composed the Gadya Traya in praise of this deity. The other three are all Shaiva foundations of the Tamil country, which makes the item a test of tradition rather than of geography.

question: The biography of Shaikh Muinuddin Chishti, authored by Jahanara, is known as
source_explanation_raw: Correct: A, Munis al Arwah. Jahanara, the eldest daughter of Shah Jahan and Mumtaz Mahal, made a pilgrimage to Ajmer in 1643 in her father's company and wrote an account of the shrine and its saint titled Munis al Arwah , The Confidant of Spirits: a biography of Shaikh Muinuddin Chishti , founder of the Chishti order in India. It is also a remarkable first-person record of a Mughal princess's pilgrimage. She describes not sleeping on a leopard skin, not extending her feet towards the sanctuary, walking barefoot from the doorway, circling the tomb seven times, and placing her own rose scarf on it. The other three titles are real works of the same broad tradition, but none of them is hers.

question: Which one of the following is not a political method of the moderates in the National Movement?
source_explanation_raw: Correct: A, Overthrow of alien rule. The Moderates who led the Indian National Congress from its founding in 1885 until the split of 1907 did not seek to end British rule; they sought to reform it and to win for India the self-government that the settler colonies already had. Their working assumption was that British rule contained institutions worth keeping and that the Government could be persuaded by argument, so their methods were constitutional throughout: resolutions at the annual sessions, petitions and memorials, deputations, questions raised through sympathetic members at Westminster, a British Committee of the Congress in London with its journal India, and a steady effort to build informed public opinion at home through the press and the platform. Their most damaging work was intellectual rather than agitational: Dadabhai Naoroji's drain of wealth argument turned poverty into an indictment of the colonial economy. The demand for an end to alien rule came later: from the Extremists after 1905 and formally from the Congress only at Lahore in 1929.

question: Swami Dayanand Saraswati took inspiration from
source_explanation_raw: Correct: B, Vedas. Dayanand Saraswati rested his entire reform programme on one claim: that the four Vedas alone are revealed and infallible, and that everything layered on top of them (image worship, the Puranic pantheon, pilgrimage, hereditary caste, child marriage, the ban on widow remarriage) is later human accretion that a reformer is free to strip away. That is the argument of his 1875 tract Satyarth Prakash, and it is why the Arya Samaj, which he founded at Bombay in April 1875, is remembered by the slogan 'Back to the Vedas'. The move is worth understanding rather than memorising: by making a text older than all the practices he disliked the sole authority, Dayanand could attack those practices from inside the tradition instead of from outside it, which is exactly what a reformer arguing with orthodox pandits needed.

question: The call for 'renunciation of (all) voluntary associations with the (British) Government' was given during
source_explanation_raw: Correct: A, Non-Cooperation Movement. The quoted phrase is lifted almost word for word from the NCERT account of 1920-22, which describes what Gandhi asked of Indians who wanted colonial rule to end: stop attending schools, colleges and law courts, stop paying taxes, and 'in sum ... adhere to a renunciation of (all) voluntary association with the (British) Government'. That word renunciation is the giveaway. Non-cooperation was defined negatively: the withdrawal of the cooperation that made British administration possible: titles handed back, government schools emptied, courts boycotted by lawyers, foreign cloth burnt, the 1919 legislature elections boycotted. It was adopted at the Calcutta special session in September 1920 and confirmed at Nagpur in December 1920, and Gandhi promised swaraj within a year if it were carried out fully.

question: Which of the following statements is/are correct with respect to Time Zone in India? 1. There is one standard time for the whole country. 2. Andaman and Nicobar Islands and Lakshadweep Islands have different Time Zones. 3. Indian Standard Time (IST) is five and half hours behind GMT. Select the correct answer using the code given below:
source_explanation_raw: Correct: A, 1 only. Statement 1 is the settled position: India keeps a single clock for the whole country, set by the standard meridian of 82°30′ East , which runs near Mirzapur in Uttar Pradesh. Statement 2 fails on the same fact. The Andaman and Nicobar Islands and Lakshadweep keep Indian Standard Time, although the Andamans lie about 10 degrees of longitude east of the standard meridian and Lakshadweep about 10 degrees west of it. Sunrise in Port Blair comes roughly an hour and a half before sunrise in Kavaratti while both clocks read the same. Statement 3 gets the arithmetic right and the direction wrong . At 15 degrees to the hour, 82°30′ is five and a half hours, but the meridian is east of Greenwich, so Indian Standard Time runs ahead of Greenwich Mean Time, not behind it.

question: D had recently visited Khardung La, Nubra Valley and several Buddhist monasteries. Which one of the following States / UT had she visited?
source_explanation_raw: Correct: D, Ladakh. All three landmarks in the stem sit within a day's drive of Leh. Khardung La is the pass on the Ladakh range that carries the road north out of Leh; the Nubra valley lies beyond it, at the meeting of the Nubra and Shyok rivers, with Diskit and its cliffside monastery on one side and the sand dunes of Hunder on the other; and the monastic landscape the question gestures at (Hemis, Thiksey, Alchi, Lamayuru, Diskit) is Ladakh's most recognisable feature. The stem's slightly odd phrasing, 'States / UT', is deliberate: Ladakh ceased to be part of the State of Jammu and Kashmir on 31 October 2019 and has been a Union Territory since, so at the time of this paper Ladakh was the only Union Territory that could answer the question at all.

question: Which one of the following States receives rainfall from both the Arabian Sea branch and the Bay of Bengal branch of Monsoon?
source_explanation_raw: Correct: A, Punjab. The south-west monsoon reaches India in two arms, and Punjab is where both of them arrive. The Bay of Bengal arm enters Bengal from the south and south-east, is turned west by the Himalaya, and, in NCERT's words, 'moves westward along the Ganga plains reaching as far as the Punjab plains'. The Arabian Sea arm splits into three, and the third of those strikes Saurashtra and Kachchh, crosses west Rajasthan along the Aravalli with very little rain to give, and then, again in NCERT's words, 'in Punjab and Haryana, it too joins the Bay of Bengal branch. These two branches, reinforced by each other, cause rains in the western Himalayas.' Punjab, in other words, is the meeting ground, which is why it is the answer even though it is far from the wettest of the four States listed.

question: Inceptisols, Entisols, Vertisols and Mollisols are orders of which one of the following?
source_explanation_raw: Correct: B, Soil. Inceptisols, Entisols, Vertisols and Mollisols are four of the twelve orders of the United States Department of Agriculture's soil taxonomy, the classification used for soil mapping across much of the world including India's national soil survey. The suffix is the tell: every order in that scheme ends in -sol, from the Latin solum for soil, and the stem before it names what makes the order distinctive. Entisols are so young or so freshly deposited that no horizons have developed; Inceptisols have only the beginnings of a horizon; Vertisols are the cracking clay soils that swell when wet and shrink when dry, turning the profile over on itself; Mollisols are the deep, soft, base-rich soils of grasslands. Nothing about sugarcane, coal or copper is classified in orders of this kind.

question: S had witnessed contour bunding and contour ploughing while visiting one of the States in India. Identify the State from the options given below.
source_explanation_raw: Correct: C, Himachal Pradesh. Both practices in the stem are answers to the same problem (water running downhill fast enough to carry the topsoil with it) and that problem exists on slopes. Ploughing along the contour instead of up and down it turns every furrow into a small barrier across the line of flow, and a contour bund does the same job with a raised earth embankment built along the contour. Of the four States offered, only Himachal Pradesh is hill country; NCERT makes the link explicit when it says the western and central Himalaya have well-developed terrace farming, and the western Himalaya is where Himachal Pradesh sits. Punjab and Haryana are flat alluvial plains where the working problems are waterlogging, salinity and over-irrigation, and Rajasthan's western districts lose soil to wind rather than to running water.

question: Which one of the following target groups is the beneficiary of 'Garib Kalyan Rojgar Abhiyan' scheme?
source_explanation_raw: Correct: B, All returning migrants. The Garib Kalyan Rojgar Abhiyaan was launched on 20 June 2020, in the months after the first national lockdown, for one clearly identified group: workers who had left the cities and gone back to their home villages . It ran as a 125-day campaign with an outlay of about fifty thousand crore rupees across 116 districts in six States, chosen because they had received the largest numbers of returning workers. The eligibility test was therefore having come back , not being female, not being below the poverty line, and not being a new arrival in a town.

question: Match List I with List II and select the correct answer using the code given below the lists : List I (Curve) A. Lorenz curve B. Phillips curve C. Engel curve D. Laffer curve List II (Indication) 1. Inflation and employment 2. Tax rates and tax revenue 3. Inequality in distribution of income or wealth 4. Income and proportion of expenditure on food Code :
source_explanation_raw: Correct: C, 3 1 4 2. Each curve is named after the economist who drew it, and each plots one pair of variables. The Lorenz curve plots the cumulative share of income or wealth against the cumulative share of population, so the gap between the curve and the 45-degree line of perfect equality measures inequality, that is indication 3. The Phillips curve plots the rate of wage or price inflation against unemployment and traces the short-run trade-off between them: indication 1. The Engel curve plots household spending on a good against income, and Engel's law is the observation that the proportion of income spent on food falls as income rises: indication 4. The Laffer curve plots tax revenue against the tax rate, and argues that revenue rises, peaks and then falls as the rate keeps climbing, since a hundred per cent rate would raise nothing: indication 2. So A-3, B-1, C-4, D-2.

question: Which one of the following is a typical example of monopolistic competition?
source_explanation_raw: Correct: B, Market for soaps. Monopolistic competition has three defining marks: many sellers, a product that each seller differentiates from the others, and free entry and exit. Soap is the textbook case in India: dozens of firms, every bar branded, perfumed and priced a little differently, heavy advertising because differentiation is the whole strategy, and nothing to stop a new brand appearing. Because the products are close but not perfect substitutes, each maker faces a downward-sloping demand curve and has a little pricing power, but free entry keeps long-run profits thin. That combination of many sellers plus differentiation is what the question is testing.

question: Following the Constitution (One Hundred and First Amendment) Act, 2016, the Parliament of India enacted quite a few GST Acts in the year 2017. Which one of the following does not fall in this category?
opt_a: The Central Goods and Services Tax Act
opt_b: The Integrated Goods and Services Tax Act
opt_c: The Goods and Services Tax (Compensation to States) Acts
opt_d: The State Goods and Services Tax Act
source_explanation_raw: Correct: D, The State Goods and Services Tax Act. The Constitution (One Hundred and First Amendment) Act, 2016 inserted Article 246A, and that article deliberately gives the power to two legislatures rather than one: 'Parliament, and, subject to clause (2), the Legislature of every State, have power to make laws with respect to goods and services tax imposed by the Union or by such State.' So the Union side of the tax was legislated by Parliament in 2017 through the Central Goods and Services Tax Act, the Integrated Goods and Services Tax Act, the Union Territory Goods and Services Tax Act and the Goods and Services Tax (Compensation to States) Act: all four assented to in April 2017. The State side was legislated separately by each State's own legislature, each passing its own State Goods and Services Tax Act. That is the one Parliament did not enact.

question: Which one of the following is not correct in respect of Directorate of Enforcement?
opt_a: It is a specialized financial investigation agency under the Department of Revenue, Ministry of Finance.
opt_b: It enforces the Foreign Exchange Management Act, 1999.
opt_c: It enforces the Prevention of Money Laundering Act, 2002.
opt_d: It enforces the Prohibition of Benami Property Transaction Act, 1988.
source_explanation_raw: Correct: D, It enforces the Prohibition of Benami Property Transaction Act, 1988. That is the statement that does not hold. The Directorate of Enforcement's own account of itself lists three enforcement statutes (the Prevention of Money Laundering Act, 2002, the Foreign Exchange Management Act, 1999 and the Fugitive Economic Offenders Act, 2018) together with the residual work still arising under the repealed Foreign Exchange Regulation Act, 1973. The benami law is not among them. It is administered by the Income Tax Department under the Central Board of Direct Taxes, which runs the initiating officers, approving and adjudicating authorities the Act creates. The other three statements are accurate, including the first: the Directorate is a specialised financial investigation agency under the Department of Revenue in the Ministry of Finance.

question: Which one of the following is not correct?
opt_a: Taxes on agricultural income is a subject under the State List.
opt_b: Price control is a subject under the Concurrent List.
opt_c: Insurance does not come under the Union List.
opt_d: 'Forests' is a subject under the Concurrent List.
source_explanation_raw: Correct: C, Insurance does not come under the Union List. That statement is false, and in a question asking which one is not correct, the false statement is the answer. Insurance is Entry 47 of the Union List in the Seventh Schedule, and has been since 1950, which is why insurance regulation, the nationalisations of 1956 and 1972 and the later opening of the sector to private and foreign capital were all done by Parliament rather than by the States. The other three statements are accurate as printed: taxes on agricultural income are Entry 46 of the State List, price control is Entry 34 of the Concurrent List, and forests are Entry 17A of the Concurrent List, having been moved there from the State List by the Constitution (Forty-second Amendment) Act, 1976.

question: Which one of the following statements is not correct about the nature of India's federal system?
opt_a: There is no equality of representation of States in the Council of States.
opt_b: Sikkim was not initially included in the Union as a full-fledged State.
opt_c: Special provisions have been laid down in the Constitution of India for Andhra Pradesh under Article 371 D.
opt_d: The Constitution of India enables the federal government to acquire the strength of a unitary system during emergencies.
source_answer_raw: This question was cancelled by the commission (marks awarded to all).
source_explanation_raw: This question was dropped. UPSC's official answer key for CDS (II) 2021 General Knowledge carries no correct option against it, and every candidate was treated alike. The reason is visible on the page: the stem asks which statement is not correct about the nature of India's federal system, and all four statements are defensible as true , so there is nothing left for the key to mark. The item could only have been repaired by rewriting statement (b) to assert that Sikkim was initially included as a full-fledged State.

question: The Constitution of India guarantees freedom of speech and expression. But the freedom is subject to certain reasonable restrictions imposed by the State. These restrictions may relate to which of the following? 1. Defamation 2. Decency or morality 3. Incitement to an offence Select the correct answer using the code given below:
source_explanation_raw: Correct: D, 1, 2 and 3. Article 19(2) lists eight grounds on which the State may impose reasonable restrictions on freedom of speech and expression, and all three items in the stem are among them. The clause allows restriction 'in the interests of the sovereignty and integrity of India, the security of the State, friendly relations with foreign States, public order, decency or morality, or in relation to contempt of court, defamation or incitement to an offence'. Decency or morality appears there in those exact words, and defamation and incitement to an offence close the list. Nothing has to be inferred; the three statements are three of the eight named grounds, so all of them qualify.

question: Which one of the following amendments in the Constitution of India made a Proclamation of Emergency immune from judicial review?
source_explanation_raw: Correct: C, 42nd Amendment. Assented to in December 1976 and commenced in January 1977, it belongs to the 1975-77 package that placed executive action beyond the courts, and it was the widest attack on judicial review the Constitution has seen. Its section 55 inserted Article 368(4) and (5), declaring that no amendment 'shall be called in question in any court on any ground' and that there is 'no limitation whatever' on Parliament's constituent power. It also inserted Articles 32A, 131A, 144A, 226A and 228A. These stopped the High Courts from considering the constitutional validity of central laws, stopped the Supreme Court under Article 32 from considering the validity of State laws, and required minimum benches and special majorities before a law could be struck down. On the emergency articles it made a Proclamation extendable to part of India, stretched President's rule under Article 356 from six months to one year at a time, and widened Articles 353, 358 and 359.

question: Which one of the following British officials was elevated to the position of Governor General after the Regulating Act of 1773?
source_explanation_raw: Correct: A, Warren Hastings. The Regulating Act of 1773 was Parliament's first attempt to bring the East India Company's Indian administration under some public control, and one of the things it did was to raise the Governor of Bengal to a new office, the Governor-General of Fort William in Bengal, with the Presidencies of Madras and Bombay made subordinate to him in matters of war and peace. Warren Hastings held the Bengal governorship at the time and so became the first holder of the new office, serving until 1785. The Act also gave him a Council of four, in which he could be outvoted and repeatedly was, and set up a Supreme Court at Calcutta which began work in 1774 under Sir Elijah Impey.

question: Which of the following ideas was preached by the Kherwar or Sapha Har movement of the 1870s?
opt_a: Acceptance of the Hindu pantheonic order
source_explanation_raw: Correct: B, Monotheism and internal social reform. The Kherwar movement of the 1870s, also called Sapha Har, was a movement of purification among the Santals of what is now the Santal Parganas region, associated with the leadership of Bhagirath Manjhi. Its two names carry its programme.
